MR. DISRAELI'S VACANT SEAT, At a dinner of the Wycombe Liberal Association on Tuesday Lord Carington announced that his brother, - the 'Fon. Rupert Carington, would contest Bucking- hamshire in the Liberal interest. . , From the Spectator. We do not unaerstand all this' newspaper incense • offered to the new Peer —these assertions that he has att-ined the fitting crown to his ezceptional career, ' these eulogies of the country which permits such a roan to rise by sheer force of intellect to such a height of grandeur. Mr. Disraeli has moral and intellectual defects of the .gravest kind— such defects that his permanent removal from power would be a cause of thankfulness alike to Great Britain and the world— but he is not of the poor stamp of men to whom a peerage lea culminating honour. The Premiership of Engler d must have been lowered indeed when any es Premier gains rank by accepting a title, and to Mr. Disraeli, who has created an Empress, and tossed coro- nets to followers to console them for exclusion from eubstantial power, an Earldom, which he can hold only for life, is but a decoration, less valuable than the Garter to a great noble or a Dukedom to a King. If he is chat his followers think him, if he is even what the electors at the last election declared him to be, the House of Lords receives in his entrance an honour which, in admitting him within their circle, the Peers have not the power to bestow. Mr. Disraeli deified by an Earldom Why he has had Dukes for henchmen He has not, as vuLiar ulogists are now repeating in every tone of adulation,,,eut is way to the Peerage. He cut his way long since to the Leadership of the House of Commons, and is now, for reasons of his own, leisurely stepping down to a less illustrious, though also less fatiguing post. Mr. Disraeli takes his title, he does not receive it, and the only honour done in the ease is to the somewhat dull assembly in which he does not think it unworthy of his position, in the evening of his strength, to relax himself with a seat. We do not believe in Mr. Disraeli as a fitting guide of the policy of Great Britain, ,but we will do him the - justice to believe that no scorn of ours for his adula- tors could equal the scorn that he must feel for the ill- bred sycophancy which could throw adulation into Such a form as this. In spite of the vein of delight in tawdriness which is So perceptible in his books, his speeches, and his policy, and to which ths Times of this week nekes so many sardonic allusions, Mr. Dis- raeli, who has poured such scorn on the Peers as up- start plutocrats, as men 'who did not conquer the land, and who do not defend it," who has never lost an I opportunity of telling them that, as compared with himself, they are barbarians of yesterday, who re- verences nothing but the "race" which he denies them to possess, and the intellect which he contemptuously strikes from the list of their qualifications, has not, we may be sure, given himself a British title asaCerpOtterne for ." 'honour. He has not bartered, knowingly, ase ,a coronet. Ile has but taken ermine as comfortable flannel for his old age He is not maces- . easy to his colleagues any longer. He is not want.d to manage the House of Lords, which can be guided much More easily by men of half his intellectual capa- city. end if be sesigntd to-morrow would leave no void ' that inaccepting aT eersge he has not already left. He is no longer indispensable, and he will feel that • truth with every hour of the official day. He may flatter himself till Parlisment meets that he has another power in reserve, a hold ever the people equal to that which he possessed over the Commons, a power like Palmerston'e, but he will wake to find himself de- luded. The power of Mr. Disraeli over the people was • very considerable and did without a doubt affect the result of ths last election, but it was not power of the kind which, will continue to attach to the Earl of Beaconsfield. The secret of the power was admira- tion—admiration for the intellectual gymnast, the political Leotard who could fly through the air so far, and who so seldom missed his tip. The householders enjoyed his audacity, smiled at his tergiversetions, and delighted in turns of policy which suggested some- thing of political frolicsomeness in the chief man in the State All men love surprises in politics, as all men enjoy surprises in their theatres or their novels. They were as amused with him as with Palmerston, though in a very diffetent way, the two admirations being as different as admiration for an acrobat and admiration for a great comedian. Disap- pearance kills that kind of confidence, and Mr. tDisraeli as intellectual gymnast has retired. The Earl of Beacons field cannot disport himself in that way in the Upper Chamber. The air is too dense, the imme- diate aud.ence too averse to such displays, the machi- nery too heavy to be trusted. The new Peer, believes, it is said, that he has a style of eloquence, unrevealed as yet, which will impress the Peers ; that while in the Commons they appreciate "Don Juan," in the Lords they will have admiration for "Paradise Lost." He may be right, and may be able at seventy to exchange the Ottova rime tar blank verse, but he will find that if the Peers admire his epics, which we doubt, their real taste being for the laughing humour and simple narrative of Chaucer, the English people will not; that • in -alterieg the form he has altered also the impresti in of tie verse, to which that form materially conduced. . . . Unless the Earl of Beaconsfield can not only rc aka himself, but show himself necessary to sante course of policy on which the nation has set its heart, he etill find that no longerleadiug the Commons, no longer excidog daily admiration, he will, like every jredecessor who has set him his example, be forgotten. by the people whom, except when in carrying household suffrage he threw over the traditions of his Party, he has never served. Bread is no cheaper, taxation no lighter, Britain no grander for Mr. Dhoaei And what chance is there of hi propoundiog such a police? We should say -simply none. When streisiug tor a cry in home affsi,s. he found none better than Sanitas sanitatum, otnnia samtas, and when eager to lead in foreign affairs has only to offer to a people who pray every week for deliverance from Turks the Turkish status quo. You cannot make a great policy out of a mere retusal to believe disagree- able trideuce. No man in- England grudges Mr. Disrae)i ease, if he deEiree it, "honours," it he cares about them, social rank, if he thinks that Britain has it to give, but among au Eigl'r. • ,amen, those who grudge them least are those who most desire that Lis authority should end.

AND CAREER. r, As a leader cf a party in the comparative wilderness, 'tom the death of Lord George Bentinckh, With very few intervals of water and manna until the suromer of 1866, Mr. Disraeli displayed a patience and a courage for which even the guerdon of an earldom is not too ample a recompense. He never during the most tty. ing period lost heart of hope. If hitherto he had to jockey the HOllBB ith minorities, he always seemed o see 1871 in the dirtance. To what extent this was due to foresight must always, of course, remain matter for private speculation. Disraeli, with the aspect of the Red Sea leader, ever gave himself the airs of a future deliverer. He sat so still and Sphinx-like, and seemed so constantly holding communion with spirits, that the party—had he set fire to an Act of Parliament , And deliberate', let.lairamill to cat it toilliOrllOUld

have accepted the demonstration as a thing of course. His own political friends, all the peers and head-men and soothsayers of the party, regarded him as one not of like passions with themselves—nor was he. He was on the summit of an exceedingly high mountain, and they were at various intervals doing down-hill work. The prophet let off a rocket, and the disciples cried "Hoe!" He whirled a catherine-stheel, and the disciples cried "Ho P' The supernaturalness, politically speaking, of their leader kept them in order. Be- cause he lived at Hughenden he was a country gentleTH man—he conformed outwardly to all the rites and ceremonies of the territorial aristocracy. Incidentally, in his novels, he flattered them—called them patricians extolled the gifts at their young men, the beauty of their maidens, their ancestral homes and palaces, the unrivalled constitution of quarter sessions, prize' labourers, prize pigs, wether mutton, the happy muck- , yards of our farming interests. But if we suppose that he regarded all these things in his inmost soul as any- thing beyond the beat development of clodhopping thb I England, from the time of the Heptarchy, could pro- duce, we should err and be deceived.

div.p: THE BRAVO CASE.

The foreman of thelittrylwrites from Upper Tooting as follows to the Daily Ems :—There is no doubt that Mr. Bravo was poisoned by tartar emetic. This being the cue, it appears to me that your numerous correspondents, who have "no doubt," and assume that he either committed suicide or killed himself in- advertently, have to account for the possession by him of tartar emetic, of which there is not one tittle of evidence. Surely the opinion of the j ur3", who had the opportunity of hearing all the case, and of watching i the demeanour of the witnesses, s worthy of more credence than that of those who set up a theory which they cannot prove, and who seem to make use of your columns to give vent to their disappointment that the verdict is not in accordance with their own views.

"An Apprentice of Lincoln's Inn" has sent a letter to the Daily Telegraph, in which he contends against the theory of Mr. Bravo's suicide. The writer thus summarises what he conceives to be the proba- bilitieraf the case. "If Mr. Bravo had been, as we are JAW to believe, thoroughly miserable and un- happy in his domestic relations, he yet must have known perfectly well how to free himself from his troubles, and was a man of sufficien t strength of character to take, if necessary, very bold steps. He could have obtained a judicial separation from his • wife, or have taken proceedings for doing so; or, he could have forced upon her a separation by mutual consent; or he could simply have left her, gone back to his own parents, and thrown upon her the responsi- bility of taking her own course. What we are asked to believe is that, being wretchedly unhappy in his mar- ried life, he preferred to poison himself rather than to go'his way and leave his wife to go hers; that, being a barrister, and having some acquainttince with medi- cine, he deliberately chose about the most painful of all possible methods of committing suicide; and that, being a thoroughly selfish man, who had never cared for his wife and had only married her for her money, he yet was capable of deliberately committing sui- cide because her affections were not suMciently set upon him. People who can deal with inconsistencies ox this kind can deal with anything, and ere welcome, if they please, to believe everything that Mrs. Cox has ' at any time morn or stated during the course of the inquiry.

div.p: EMBEZZLEMENT BY A NEWSPAPER , HAWKER AT LYMM.

Richard Phenix, a. young man about 20 years of •age,was charged at the Lymm Police-court, on Tuesday morning, before Mr. J. Barton, with having received certain monies belonging to John Fairclough and others, amounting to upwards of £2, and embezzling the same. Mr. John Faircloligh, landlord of the Fleece Lymm, said that he knew the prisoner. Witness ' and others were the promoters of the Lymm athletic festival. Witness was the treasurer. Messrs. Sumner, Voysey, and George Enoch Morgan were the commit- tee. He (witness) saw the prisoner on the 10th inst., when he came to see him about selling programmes. He next saw him on the following Monday, when he asked the prisoner how they generally sold pro- grammes. Ile said he had 2s. 6d. a hundred, and wit- ness said will two shillings do. Prisoner said it would. He told prisoner to deliver up the money to him or to the secretary, Mr. Hugh Harrison, he would find them both in the tent. Witness said the money was to he delivered up when they were aold. He told witness that he carried out papers for the "Guardian." He said he could sell the programmes for 3d. each. He gave prisoner bO, and he had never accounted for the money since.—Prisoner : You never told me when the money was to be paid in.—Joseph Sumner, son of the landlady of the Plough Inn, Lymm, one of the com- mittee said that he saw the prisoner on the 14th of August on the field, before the sports commenced. He was selling programmes at the time. The prisoner came to witness, and said he wanted another batch of , programmes, which consisted of 50. Subsequently he ' came for another batch, Baying "I have sold 80 at 3d." Witness gave him another bundle, and subsequently an additional one. He had in all three bundles of fifty each. He said" I sold that lot for 21," meaning that he had sold the last 50 at that price. Witness saw two other bundles given to prisoner. He received no money from the prisoner, and had not seen him since. —Cross-examined : I never mentioned the number I had Bold for 31—Henry Voysey, one of the athletic festival committee, and landlord of the Church Inn, Lymm,stated that he saw prisoner selling programmes, • one of which he purchased from him for threepence. —By prisoner: R might be twelve or half-past when I purchased the programme.—lsaao Houghton, black- smith, Lymm, stated that he bought a Programme from prisoner about two o'clock, and gave twopence for it. The prisoner asked threepence. P.C. Rowe deposed to apprehending prisoner on warrant at Latchford, on Saturday night, and charged him with selling 250 programmes, the property of Mr. Fairclough and others. He told him he had sold them, and he in- tended to return the money. He had trusted two lads with some and they went off with the money. He did not know their names and had not the full money to return, but would bring it some other time. P.S. Hollingworth stated that on Monday morning he charged the prisoner in the lock-ups with stealing £2 the monies of John Fairclough and others his masters, he said "its net that much. I sold 32 at threepence, 40 at 25. the remainder at id., only what I returned to a barmaid. I should have returned the money but I gave it to my wife and she had spent BOMB of it." The prisoners's father said that he had sold programmes at Sports, but had never had a specified time to pay the money in. The money should be refunded. The pri- • loner was reinanded far the attendance of the Secre- tary, Mr, Hugh Harrison, who stated that he had re- ceived no money from, him. The prisoner when brought up in the afternoon, was committed for trial • • but adulated to bail.

div.p: THE ALTRINOHAM SANITLEY AUTHORITY.
GOVERNMENT INQUIRY AT WILMSLOW.

Colonel Ponsonby Cox, R.E., one of the inspectors of the Local Government Board, opened an inquiry on Wednesday morning at Wilmslow into the following matters :—An application to the Local Government Board to borrow £10,400 for the sewage of Ashton- upon-Merley, a petition from the Rural Sanitary Authority of the Altrincham Union for a provisional order to enable them to take certain lauds in the parish of Wilmslow and in the township of Hale, near Altrincham, for the disposal of sewage; an application to the Local Government Board to borrow £2,600 for the sewerage of Hale, and a proposal for uniting the districts of Bollin Fee, Pownall Fee, and Fulstiaw, near Manchester, and for forming them into a local government district. The land required for the Wilmslow outran was drat considered, and was opposed by Messrs. Chadwick and. Barlow, on the ground that works of such a kind will prove injurious to their property.—Mr. Toy, the agent to the local board promoters, said the question would arise as to whether a better and cheaper plot of land would not be secured than the one on the Fownall Hall estate.— Colonel Cox said it was his Intention to see the land before he left the district. The only opposition to the application regarding Hale drainage was by Ur. Toden, of Altrinchdm, re- presenting gentlemen who have property in the dis- trict, which they apprehended would be deteriorated in value if the proposed works were to be constructed. No opposition was offered to the application for £10,400 for the drainage of Ashton-upon-Mersey, although the clerk to the Altrinchand Guardians ex- pressed some doubt as to whether the notices had been served in time to enable them to be proceeded with as early as they could wish. Mr. Toy opened the argu- ment upon tne question of the adoption of a local board for Wilmslow, and it was afterwards warmly ' supported by ,the Rev. Emery Bates, rector of Wilms- low; by the chairman of the Altrincham Board of Guardians, Ur. Ambler; by the chairman of the Sanitary Authority ; Mr. Kilvert, of the Manchester corporation • and by several other gentlemen. Mr. May, of the'Prestbury Highway Board, attended with a deputation from Macclesfield, and complained that the funds of the Highway Board would be impoverished if Wilmslow whose rateable value is one.fifth of its entire district seceded, and asked for some recompense to the remaining towvstiiLa in the Highway Board district, or that the appointment of a Loc.l Board might be delayed until some general measure affecting turnpike reads be passed by Parliament—Colonel Cox thought the question upon which NU. Mr. Editor,—Will you kindly allow me to call the attention of my fellow-townsnien—in whose breast' glow the least spark of Christian feeling—to what has been and is now going on in some of the fairest por- tions of European Turkey.

For some time 'past the thoughts of this country have been drawn to the terribly outrageous and bar barons manner in which the Turkish Government haN • thought fit to condiettie war against crushed and un- happy Servia.

The anxiety of the nation regarding the unheard of cruelties perpetrated by the Turkish horde on their victim, has to some extent found vent through the pub- lic press, and has resulted in a number of questions being put to the leading members of the Government daring the continuanos of the Parliamentary session' Mr. Disraeli notably, and Lord Derby in a less degree, have thrown discredit upon the reports which have reached us; and with the object of shielding the Tur- kish Government from public execration, merited by the indiscriminate butchery of women and children in Bulgaria. Whatever doubts we may have entertained up to the present about the massacre of the Servian people, and however much we may have hoped that the reports were exaggerated, now that the revelations of the "Daily News" special commissioner have come to hand respecting Batak, we shall be compelled to believe in the dire reality of these incredible and atrocious outrages. After reading the harrowing and ghastly details supplied by the pen of the Commis- sioner, I could not help uttering an earnest wish that ere long Russia might determine to defend the right, and put an end to a great scandal to the nations of ' Europe. In remembering what has been the attitude of England to Turkey and Servia respectively, I feel almost ashamed that I am an Englishman. Hitherto the weight of English influence has always been on the side of the oppressed, and always giving assistance in the struggle for liberty; but in this abominable war the public conscience is deeply con- cerned that the English Government has lent the weight of her infinenee to the most despotic Govern- ment in Europe, and has done her ri#Tn,st t reuler abortive the manly effort of the Serum] people to q‘rd liberty and national independence. Against the war as it is at pre...ent conducted by Turkey the voice of England ought to be heard. The blood of the murdered thousands of Servia's best sons and daughters, as well as the heartrending wail of the survivors (worse than dead), calls for sympathy from every city, borough, village, and hamlet in England. Let the people of Warrington and its neighbouring towns follow the example set at Manchester and else- where, and hasten to place on record our strongest protest against the inhuman conduct of Turkey in this struggle—conduct as mach opposed to the usages of civilised warfare as it is against the common in- stincts of humanity.

Poraticia, Neutrality las its peculiar diffi- culties, and those difficulties seem to press with peculiar force just now on a newspaper in the Warrington and Cheshire district, which has especially paraded its Neutrality, not merely in political but in religious matters. The Warrington Guardian, and the journalistic brood which it has generated; and which, by its somewhat ostentatious proclamation of its Neutrality, seems .to claim to be "a centre of political darkness," has lately begun to oscillate a little from its ostensibly stedfast determination to dis-i countenance every political party in ' thd State, and appears to be gravitating to the Conservative side. Its London correspou. dent—we will not say if it be N. or AL., bittl probably the latter—lately delivered • him.; self of the following observation :—" John Bright and his party have had 40 years outl of 45 of power and place, and might have done something to mitigate the sufferings of Dissenters if so inclined." The beauty of Neutrality is especially conspicuous in this curious observation. If Neutrality is a fine perception of the merits and demerits of diverse political schools, unobscured by any human disposition to expose this one' or that one in particular, we should greet its mani- festation as a novel if not an attractive spirit in newspaper literature. A. mother without a favourite, a man without, an Junia-I ble vice, a historian without a Fejudice,l are no doubt admirable characters, yet they suggest coldness and unattainable heighti We are not encouraged to think that tll4 Warrington Guardian means an exquisite itut sight, combined with judicial impartiality, when it ;peaks of ita neutrality. If then_ not ,by knowledge, by what can its neutrality be inspired? If a man who is absolutely ignorant as to what constitutes value ,in a precious stone is asked his opinion of the rival merits of two diamonds, surely his decision must be wonderfully neutral, although not very trustworthy. But Plato has pointed out that there are two kinds of ignorance: simple ignorance which knows nothing, and double ignorance which knowing no hing, does not even know that it knows nothing. This last appears to be the condition of mind which favours the development of political neutrality, and the fair specimen of it which we quote at the head of these lines could not be improved upon. Observe that a fairly intelligent national school boy, on being asked what the Liberal party has done for Dissent during the last half century, would have heard of Catholic Emancipation and Jewish Disabilities, even if he knew, little of Corporation and Test Acts, Church Rates and University Tests. An ignorant man, being asked the same question, would reply that he did not know. But a person gifted with the double ignorance discovered by Plato, not knowing that he does not know, volunteers a definite statement on the subject. Although the- words from the Warrington Guardian were not printed in the editorial column, can we doubt the identity of "Our London Corres- pondent," a gentleman who is the envy of rival foreign Universities (price lists on ap- plication), and who is conspicuous for th 4 condition of mind, which, as we have seen, encourages political neutrality? Yet it is scarcely desirable that so much neutrality should be sown broad-cast amongst us with- out a little counter knowledge, and we pro- pose to refresh the memories of our readers by briefly dwelling upon some of the vic- tories of religious liberty, won by John Bright's party during the last fifty years, over the united battalions of Toryism and Neutrality. That magnificent, nay sublime, maxim which consecrated the air of old Judea "Do unto others as you would have others do unto you," which, in its way, was a greater discovery, in morals, than any made by Bacon or Isaac Newton, in the physical world, might be written oi the banner of all the great and good men who, from the time of Augustus to the present hour, have engaged in the war of religious liberty, on the side of freedom. The history of this struggle is the history of contending forces of thought and—to adopt the sug- gestion of the Warrington Guardian—neu- trality. But let us first answer the question we necessarily evolve out of the insolent and baseless reproach of "Our London corres- pondent " : "What has John Bright and his party done during the last 50 years to mitigate the' sufferings of Dissenters " ? There is a strange sound about the words whi&i suggest the idea that Greenville Uni- versity may have sent a Medical Doctor's degree by mistake and that the new prac- titioner was trying his hand at diagnosis. However our answer to the question is this. During the last fifty years, Dissent has been almost completely freed from the persecution and the oppression to whioh it has been subject ever since the establishment of a State Church in England. With one ex- ception every one of the repeals necessary to bring about this freedom have been recom- mended and carried by John Bright's party, in opposition to every other party under whatever name it has existed. By the way we hear that an ingenious explanation of newspaper neutrality was given lately in a public: room in Warrington. Some person asked why a neutral paper gave expression t so much covert conversation, and the ap- parently irrelevant reply was that a Jesuit is formidable in proportion to the success of his disguise. Well, being more responsible than "Our London correspondent" for the statements we make, let us proceed to sub- stantiate the one that we have put forward. But as a preliminary let us pay a passing tribute to the men who during that long interval of religious strife which was , bequeathed by Henry VIII. and Elizabeth to nine generations of men,'"and which is only now dying with the reluetance of one who has no hope of a resurrection. Let us take down the armour of these brave warriors who sacrificed home and wealth and even human life on the most splendid battle fields that bad passions have ever sought, let us take it ciLl'n and burnish it with the enthusiasm of true 75.'Yerence., until we obtain some faint reflection of the Cipirit of the Puritan and the self-denial of the Non- conformist, the humanitarianism of the Jew, and the courage of the Catholic. One likes to think of the brave battalion of English ministers, two thousand strong, who relin- quished everything which makes this life pleasant, rather than subscribe to the Act of Uniformity, as the proFenitors of that Liberal party which, by just and constitu- tional .'means, has completely reversed the styli; Of religious warfare carried on by the Stuarts, by o,eans ,which were neither just be it remembered nor constitutional. For, that while such Acts of Parliament as the Corporation Act, which prohibited a man from holding a corporate office unless he had taken the sacrament within' a year: another Act, by which no one could serve as a vestry- man unless he engaged to conform to the ; the Five Mile Act, which forbade a Ntuorngyconformist , minister to within five Li miles of a corporate town t the Conventicle Act, which punished attendance at meetings of more thiui MI peons, in any house? for
